founded.what: The year the first bottles of Brut Gold left the Cattier family's cellars: the brand dates itself from its first release, not from a house of its own.

kind.means: A négociant manipulant, a house in the trade's own word: the Cattier family's house grows grapes, buys more and makes the wine itself, and makes Armand de Brignac as a brand.

story: Armand de Brignac is a brand, not an old house. It is made by the Cattier family, who by the brand's account have made wine at Chigny-les-Roses, on the Montagne de Reims, since 1763; the family's own house dates its first vines there to 1625. In the 1950s, by the family's account, a mother of the family came upon a character called Monsieur de Brignac in a novel and registered the name for a wine to come. It lay unused for half a century. In 2006 the first bottles of Brut Gold left the Cattier cellars, dressed in a metallised gold bottle with a pewter ace of spades on the front, and the nickname Ace of Spades followed. In November 2014 the remaining stake held by Sovereign Brands, a New York firm, was bought out and the brand passed to a single owner. In February 2021 Moët Hennessy bought half of the brand, with an agreement to distribute it across the world, and the Cattier family went on making the wine. The range grew beyond Brut Gold to a Rosé, a Blanc de Blancs, a Blanc de Noirs and a Demi Sec. The wines age in the family's cellars under Rilly-la-Montagne, almost thirty metres deep by the family's account.

style.line: Round, ripe and generous rather than lean: a blend of three harvests, made only from the first juice of the press and finished with a moderate dosage.
style.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Meunier in Brut Gold: the house's sheets have moved from equal Pinot Noir and Chardonnay with a fifth of Meunier to half Pinot Noir, two fifths Chardonnay and a tenth of Meunier.
style.reserve: Reserve wine from two older harvests goes into every blend of three, by the house's sheets; its share is not settled here.
style.lees: The house's pages read give no time on its lees for Brut Gold; merchants' figures run from three years to six.
style.dosage: 9 grams a litre for Brut Gold, by the house, the liqueur itself of base wine aged a year in French oak, by the house's account.

nv.name: Brut Gold
nv.note: Here the prestige cuvée is itself the wine a guest knows: Brut Gold, the gold bottle, carries no vintage, and it was the brand's first and for a time its only wine.

cuvee.name: Brut Gold

first.what: The year of the first release: Brut Gold blends three harvests and so has no first vintage.

cuvee.rhythm: Made since 2006 as a blend of three harvests for each release: an older sheet of the house names the 2009, 2010 and 2012 harvests.
cuvee.blend: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Meunier: about half Pinot Noir, two fifths Chardonnay and a tenth Meunier on the house's current page, where an older sheet gave equal Pinot Noir and Chardonnay with a fifth Meunier.
cuvee.sites: The sheets read name no villages for the blend. The Cattier family's own vines lie at Chigny-les-Roses on the Montagne de Reims, and the cellars beneath Rilly-la-Montagne.
cuvee.making: Only the first, gentlest juice of the press, the part the trade calls the cuvée, goes into the wine, by the house. Three harvests are blended, the base year with reserve wine of two older ones. The dosage is 9 grams a litre, its liqueur of base wine aged a year in French oak, by the house's account. Each bottle is then finished by hand with its pewter label and polished, and the metallised glass shields the wine from light.
cuvee.lees: The house's pages read give no figure; merchants' listings say three years at least, four to five, or six.
cuvee.bottle: The metallised gold bottle, which by the house's account also shields the wine from light, carries a pewter label in the shape of an ace of spades, applied by hand; the nickname Ace of Spades comes from it.
cuvee.young: Peach and orange blossom over a touch of lemon, with vanilla, honey and brioche on a round, creamy palate and a long finish of fine acidity.
cuvee.aged: It is released ready to drink, the honey and vanilla already there; neither the house nor a critic read describes a bottle kept long after release, so how it ages is not told here.
cuvee.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius, the Codex's range for sparkling wine; no need to decant; a tulip or a white wine glass, with the bottle shown at the table.

table.house45: Armand de Brignac is a Champagne brand, not an old house, first released in 2006. It is made by the Cattier family of Chigny-les-Roses, on the Montagne de Reims, who date their winemaking there to 1763. The name came from a character in a novel, registered by the family in the 1950s for a wine to come. Guests know it by the bottle, metallised gold with a pewter ace of spades on the front, which is why many call it Ace of Spades. Moët Hennessy bought half the brand in 2021, and the family went on making it. Brut Gold is the wine that started it all.
table.house10: Armand de Brignac is the gold bottled Champagne brand of 2006, made by the Cattier family of Chigny-les-Roses.
table.cuvee45: Brut Gold is the first wine of Armand de Brignac, released in 2006, and the one in the gold bottle. It blends Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Meunier from three harvests, so it carries no vintage. The young year is blended with reserve wine from two older ones. Only the first, gentlest juice of the press goes in, and that makes it round and generous rather than lean. In the glass you find peach, orange blossom and honey, with a touch of lemon. I pour it at about nine degrees in a tulip glass, and I bring the bottle to the table so you can see it.
table.sale: If the table is celebrating, Brut Gold arrives in its gold bottle and pours round and generous, with peach and honey. Shall I bring one out so everyone can see it?
table.cuvee10: Brut Gold is Armand de Brignac's gold bottled Champagne, a blend of three harvests made by the Cattier family.
table.cuvee20: Brut Gold is the wine that launched Armand de Brignac in 2006, made by the Cattier family on the Montagne de Reims. It blends three harvests of Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Meunier, and it tastes of peach, orange blossom and honey.

guests.q: Is this the Ace of Spades?
guests.a: Yes, that is its nickname, from the pewter ace of spades on the bottle. The label itself reads Armand de Brignac, and the wine is Brut Gold.
The Cattier family of Chigny-les-Roses, on the Montagne de Reims, who date their winemaking there to 1763. Moët Hennessy bought half the brand in 2021, and the family went on making the wine.
No. Brut Gold blends three harvests, the base year with reserve wine from two older years, so the label carries no vintage.

traps: Ace of Spades is the nickname for the pewter emblem, not the name on the label: the label reads Armand de Brignac, and the wine Brut Gold.
Armand de Brignac is a brand first released in 2006, not a historic house; the Cattier family behind it has owned vines since 1763.
By the Cattier family's account the name comes from a character in a novel, not from a founder or a place.
The class sheet's NV is the trade's shorthand for non vintage and is not printed on the label: Brut Gold is a blend of three harvests.

questions.q: A guest asks for the Champagne in the gold bottle with a pewter ace of spades. Which wine do you bring?
questions.exp: Brut Gold of Armand de Brignac wears the metallised gold bottle and the pewter ace of spades. Cristal is Louis Roederer's in clear glass, Belle Epoque is Perrier-Jouët's with its anemones, and Palmes d'Or is Nicolas Feuillatte's.

questions.q: By the Cattier family's account, where does the name Armand de Brignac come from?
opts: A village of the Montagne de Reims
questions.exp: By the family's account the name came from a character in a novel, registered in the 1950s and first used in 2006. It is no founder's name and no place: the family's village is Chigny-les-Roses.

questions.q: Why does a bottle of Brut Gold carry no vintage on its label?
opts: Its grapes come from outside Champagne
A gold bottle may not show a year
questions.exp: Brut Gold blends three harvests, the base year with reserve wine from two older years, so no single year can be printed. Its grapes are Champagne's own, and the bottle has nothing to do with it.

report: kind.code: the letters NM were not read on a label; a profile says the French authorities list the brand as a négociant manipulant and a rating site lists the Cattier house as NM, so the code stands as an inference.

The 2014 buy out of Sovereign Brands rests on Decanter of November 2014 and Wikipedia; the February 2021 half share and the family's making on, on Decanter and The Drinks Business of February 2021, both cited by addresses that name nobody.
The living owner of the brand from 2014 and the family members who make it are never named; the story says the stake was bought out and the brand passed to a single owner.
The 1763 date is the brand's and the library's; the Cattier house's own page dates the family's first vines at Chigny-les-Roses to 1625, and the story gives both as accounts.

Left out for want of a stated source: the time Brut Gold spends on its lees (merchants say three, four to five or six years, and the record says so), and whether the base wines see oak or go through malolactic, so style.vessels and style.malolactic are empty.

The oak aged liqueur is now the dosage, by the house's own account (base wine of the harvest aged a year in French oak); the half share of reserve wine, a quarter from each of two older years, was not found by the refuter and was cut, the record saying only that reserve wine of two older harvests goes in.
Left out: a listing that calls Rilly-la-Montagne, Chigny-les-Roses and Ludes Grand Cru villages, which they are not, so no villages are given for the blend.

The blend moved between the house's sheets (40, 40 and 20 per cent on an older sheet, 50, 40 and 10 on the current page), so the record gives both in words; a merchant's 9.5 grams a litre stands against the house's 9, and the house's figure is kept.
The aged glass is not invented: no note of a bottle kept long after release was found.

No tension with the library: the record keeps its 2006, 1763, the novel and the pewter ace of spades; the library calls the Cattier cellars among the deepest in Champagne and the record gives the family's own almost thirty metres instead.

changed: The half share of reserve wine, a quarter from each of two older harvests, was cut from style.line, style.reserve, cuvee.making, cuvee45, a guest's answer, the term card and the cuvee question: no source read by the refuter states it, and one merchant gives 10 to 50 per cent; three harvests stand, by the house's sheets.
The term card's front and back were reworded before the freeze to ask for the three harvests and why no year is printed, since the half share it asked for was cut.

style.dosage and cuvee.making gain the house's own account of its liqueur, base wine aged a year in French oak, which settles the author's doubt over dosage or tirage; the Blanc de Noirs and Rosé figures left the dosage field.
cuvee.rhythm drops the merchant's 2012, 2013 and 2014 harvests, whose listing left the sources; the house's older sheet's 2009, 2010 and 2012 stay.
